name: The Teaching-Screen Recorder
oneLiner: Drives the app's teaching mode, scrapes the classification labels the assistant renders on-screen — and only on-screen — and asserts them against expectations, PII guardrail included.
lead: In teaching mode a user submits text and the assistant classifies it into on-screen labels — topic, IT-relevance percentage, audience fields, business-org. Those labels render only in the DOM, never in the API/data feed. This agent drives the flow via Playwright, scrapes every label off the page, screenshots it, and asserts each result against the expected outcome.
chore: The manual version: paste each sample into the teaching screen, wait for classification, then eyeball the labels — topic tags, the IT-relevance percentage, the audience fields, the business-org dropdown — write them down, screenshot. Across ten curated samples it's slow, and it's easy to misread a chip or forget to scroll to a field.
instead: The agent walks every sample: submits the text, waits for classification to finish, scrapes every label off the DOM, captures a full-page screenshot, and asserts each result matches expectation. You get a PASS/FAIL/WARN report for the whole batch.
whyItMatters: If the assistant mislabels an internal document — say, tagging a security policy as non-IT — it gets routed to the wrong people, so verifying the labels protects how content gets shared.

howItWorks.step: Clicks the teaching-mode skill card to start a fresh sample — dragging through a swipeable carousel if the card isn't visible.
howItWorks.explain: The teaching card may be present-but-off-screen in a swipeable carousel, so this is **try-visible-first, then swipe-and-retry**. `SEL.teachingCard` is a *list* of selectors iterated in order, so a markup change that renames the card still matches via an alternate selector. The physical swipe is a real drag — `mouse.move` to the right edge, `down`, `move` to the left edge with `{ steps: 10 }` so the motion is **incremental** (a single jump can fail to register as a swipe gesture), then `up` — and after each of up to **8** swipes it re-checks every card selector, clicking the instant one becomes visible. Both `isVisible` calls are `.catch(() => false)` so a transient miss just continues the loop rather than throwing. It returns `false` after 8 fruitless swipes, letting the caller report 'card not found' instead of hanging.

howItWorks.step: Submits the sample and waits for the 'Generating Summary' and 'Thinking' indicators to appear and then fully clear before scraping anything.
howItWorks.explain: This is a **rising-then-falling-edge** wait, and the asymmetry is the whole point. `Promise.race` on the *visible* state means it proceeds as soon as **any one** of the three indicators appears — that confirms classification actually started, guarding against a race where the code reads the DOM before the assistant has begun. `Promise.all` on the *hidden* state then requires **every** indicator to clear, because the app shows different ones at different phases and the answer isn't done until all are gone. Every `waitFor` is `.catch(() => {})` so a **never-appearing** indicator can't fail the run — for instance, a cached instant classification might never show 'Thinking', and swallowing that lets the flow continue rather than hang for the full timeout. The trailing fixed `waitForTimeout(5000)` is a pragmatic settle: the indicators vanish a beat before the labels (chips, percentages) finish painting, so scraping too early would miss fields.

howItWorks.step: Parses the IT-relevance percentage from the assistant's response text — only an explicit 'Information Technology' result counts, any other named category reads as 0% IT.
howItWorks.explain: The subtlety here is that the page always shows *a* percentage next to *some* category, and naively grabbing the first number would conflate '90% Marketing' with a high IT score. So it anchors the regex to the **literal phrase 'Information Technology'** — only `X% Information Technology` is read as the real IT score. When a *different* named category carries the percentage, it returns a hard **`0`** (the sample is confidently non-IT), which is deliberately distinct from the third case: no recognized category at all returns **`null`** (couldn't read it). That `0` vs `null` distinction flows into the verdict — `0` can legitimately mean 'correctly not IT', while `null` signals a scrape failure to investigate. `\d{1,3}` bounds the match to a plausible 0–100 percentage, and `parseInt(..., 10)` pins base-10 so a leading zero is never read as octal.

howItWorks.step: Scrapes the audience fields — business line, region, corporate function, role — trying several selector strategies per field since the DOM markup varies.
howItWorks.explain: The audience chips render through component-library elements whose markup isn't stable, so each field is resolved by a **layered selector fallback**: first the semantic `form-field:has(field-label…)` structure, and only if that yields zero chips does it fall back to the looser `label…` + `xpath=..` (walk to the parent) approach. Anchoring by the field's **visible label text** rather than a positional/CSS path is what lets the same code read all four fields and survive re-ordering. Each chip's text is `.catch(() => '')`-guarded and `.trim()`-ed, and only **non-empty** values are pushed, so a stray empty chip node doesn't pollute the results. The final safety net keys off `result.region.length === 0` as a proxy for 'all DOM strategies failed' and drops to raw-text parsing — chosen because Region is the field most reliably present when classification truly succeeded, so its absence is a good signal the structured scrape came up empty.

howItWorks.step: Asserts each captured result against the sample's expectation — including a targeted check that the seeded-PII sample trips the privacy guardrail and no other sample trips it.
howItWorks.explain: The PII sample is judged by an **inverted rule**, and the two branches use deliberately different match strictness. For non-PII samples, an unexpected guardrail trip is a **`WARN`, not a `FAIL`** — a false-positive privacy flag is a real signal worth surfacing but shouldn't hard-fail a run, and it's detected by the app's **exact** banner string ('pii or conflicts have been detected') to avoid over-matching innocent prose. The PII sample uses a **broad** regex (`pii|personal|sensitive|redact|privacy`) instead, because a missed guardrail is a genuine privacy incident and you want the widest reasonable evidence that *some* protection fired — here a miss is a hard **`FAIL`**. The ordinary case gates on `itClassificationPct >= 70`, and the `?? 0` matters: recall a `null` percentage means scrape failure, and `?? 0` coerces it below threshold to `WARN` rather than letting `null >= 70` slip through — a sample whose labels couldn't be read is flagged for review, never silently passed.

examples.caption: An IT topic that should classify as IT
examples.input: A paragraph on a team's cloud setup and zero-trust security, submitted in teaching mode.
examples.output: The agent scrapes '100% Information Technology', tags 'Infrastructure Services', and the matching audience fields. PASS — classified as IT with all fields captured.

examples.caption: A non-IT topic that must NOT classify as IT
examples.input: A paragraph on employee wellness programs and office ergonomics.
examples.output: The agent scrapes a low IT percentage (under 70%) and marks PASS — 'correctly classified as non-IT', confirming no over-tagging.

examples.caption: A sample seeded with PII
examples.input: Text including a fake new hire's name, SSN, personal email, and home address.
examples.output: The agent checks the response mentions privacy, sensitive data, or redaction. If it does, PASS — the guardrail fired. If the details pass through untouched, FAIL — the guardrail missed.

underHood.heading: Opens teaching mode
underHood.whenRuns: Once, at the start of each sample.
underHood.input: The teaching-mode skill card, possibly hidden in a swipeable carousel.
underHood.output: A fresh chat screen ready to accept a pasted sample.

underHood.heading: Submits the sample and waits
underHood.output: A finished classification — the agent waits for the 'Generating Summary' and 'Thinking' indicators to appear and then fully clear before reading.

underHood.heading: Scrapes every label off the DOM
underHood.input: The rendered page — these labels never appear in the API/data feed, only in the DOM.
underHood.output: Topic tags, IT-relevance percentage, audience fields (business line, region, function, role), and the business-org dropdown — read through layered selectors with a raw-text fallback.

underHood.heading: Checks the privacy guardrail
underHood.output: PASS if it mentions privacy, sensitive data, or redaction; FAIL if the PII passes through untouched.

underHood.heading: Assigns PASS/FAIL/WARN/ERROR
underHood.whenRuns: After each sample is fully scraped.
underHood.input: The captured labels plus the sample's expected outcome.
underHood.output: A verdict with a one-line reason, saved into the report alongside a full-page screenshot.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
An app login that can open its teaching-mode skill.
A one-time interactive sign-in on first run (so the agent can persist the storage-state and reuse it after).
Ten built-in sample texts ship with the agent — including one seeded with PII to exercise the privacy guardrail — so no content prep is required to start.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime the agent runs on.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a TypeScript program; Node executes it. One-time setup per machine.
steps.firstRun: Only needed on a fresh machine.

steps.label: Install the agent's dependencies, then Playwright in its sibling folder.
steps.cmd:
cd path/to/the-agents
npm install

# the browser-clicking library lives in its own sibling folder:
cd Playwright
npm install
steps.why: The root install pulls the base-agent framework and the dotenv config loader. The second pulls in Playwright, which pastes each sample, waits for classification, and scrapes every label off the DOM.
steps.firstRun: Downloads everything (a minute or two, longer the first time Playwright fetches its Chromium binary).

steps.label: (Optional) set an SSO password in `.env` if your login uses one.
steps.cmd:
# in a .env file at the project root:
SSO_PASSWORD=your-password
steps.why: On a redirect to a company SSO page the agent tries this password automatically. Leave it unset and sign in by hand the first time — either way the storage-state gets saved for next time.

steps.label: First run: one sample, headed, to complete sign-in.
steps.why: A visible Chromium window opens, clicks the teaching-mode card, pastes sample #1, and waits for classification before scraping every label. Running one sample first confirms sign-in works before the full batch.
steps.firstRun: A browser opens; sign in when prompted, then the run continues on its own.

steps.label: Real run: the full batch.
steps.cmd:
npm run teach:capture

# or against a different environment:
npm run teach:capture:qa
steps.why: Runs every built-in sample end-to-end: submits the text, waits for the topic tags, IT-relevance percentage, and audience fields to render, screenshots the full page, and asserts the PII sample tripped the guardrail.
steps.rerun: Reuses the saved login. Each run re-tests every sample fresh — use `--prompts 1,2,4` to target just a few.

steps.label: Open the report and screenshots.
steps.why: The JSON holds every sample's captured labels and a PASS/FAIL/WARN/ERROR verdict with a one-line reason; the screenshots folder has a full-page image per sample (plus an `-error` image if one failed) for a human to eyeball.

inputs.name: --env <dev|qa>
inputs.desc: Which environment to run the samples against.

inputs.name: --prompts <ids>
inputs.desc: Run only specific sample numbers, comma-separated (default: all).

inputs.name: --headless
inputs.desc: Run invisibly in the background instead of showing the browser window.

inputs.name: --timeout <ms>
inputs.desc: How long to wait for classification before giving up (default 180000ms).

inputs.name: environment variables (.env)
inputs.desc: An optional SSO password, only if your login has one.

outputs.name: TeachApp_Capture_<timestamp>.json
outputs.desc: Every sample's captured topic tags, IT-relevance percentage, audience fields, business-org value, and a PASS/FAIL/WARN/ERROR verdict with reason.

outputs.name: test<N>.png
outputs.desc: A full-page screenshot of the finished classification screen for each sample.

outputs.name: test<N>-error.png
outputs.desc: Captured instead, only if that sample's run threw an error.

runbook.rerun: No fingerprinting — every run re-submits every selected sample from scratch. What's reused is the login: once saved, later runs (even `--headless`) skip signing in. Use `--prompts` to re-check just the samples you care about.
runbook.integrate: Run the full batch after any change to the classification logic or its prompt, and diff the PASS/FAIL/WARN counts against the last run. The one PII-seeded sample is the most important regression to watch — if its guardrail stops firing, that's a privacy incident waiting to happen, not a cosmetic miss.

video.caption: A 3-4 minute screen recording: watch the agent paste a sample into teaching mode and read every label the assistant fills in.
script: Open a terminal beside the app so viewers see the browser the agent controls.
Say: 'This agent checks how the assistant sorts submitted text into on-screen labels — labels that never show up in the plain data feed. Watch.'
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; one line on what Node is.
Show the two `npm install` runs — the agent's own libraries, then the browser-automation library in its sibling folder.
Mention the optional sign-in password file, then say most people just log in by hand the first time.
Run the single-sample command; narrate the teaching-mode card being clicked and the sample text being pasted in.
Point out the 'Generating Summary' / 'Thinking' indicators, then their disappearance — that's the sort finishing.
Show the topic tags, IT-relevance percentage, and audience fields being read straight off the screen.
Run the full batch; call out the one sample seeded with fake personal details and the privacy check that follows.
Open the JSON report and a screenshot; point at a PASS and, if present, a WARN or FAIL with its one-line reason.
Close: 'Ten samples, every label read and checked, in the time it'd take a person to do just one by hand.'
